desc: A tune from musicals or popular song that jazz musicians have repeatedly performed and recorded. Often called "The Great American Songbook," standards serve as a shared vocabulary and foundation for improvisation.
A new melody written over the chord changes of an existing standard. Widely used in the bebop era as a way to try out new lines over familiar "rhythm changes"-style progressions.
The piano or guitar playing chords behind a soloist. More than mere accompaniment, comping is a rhythmic and harmonic dialogue with the soloist.
A format where multiple players alternate soloing every four bars. Often used to close out a session, especially in exchanges between a drummer and horn players.
A session format where players of the same instrument compete to outdo one another's improvisation. A proving ground used by both swing-era big-band players and bebop musicians.
The sequence of chords underlying a tune, often simply called "the changes." Jazz improvisation is distinguished by building melodic lines while tracking this progression in real time.
A bass line built mainly on quarter notes, moving smoothly between chord tones to outline the harmony while keeping steady time. The rhythmic backbone of swing and post-bebop rhythm sections.

The flattened third, fifth, or seventh degree of a major scale. Rooted in the blues, these notes give jazz its characteristic "cry" and pitch bend. The label of the same name, Blue Note Records, is also famed as a hard bop powerhouse.
A structure where one phrase (the call) is answered by another (the response). Deeply rooted in African American music generally, it appears vividly in gospel and soul jazz.
A phrase used to describe improvisation: rather than reproducing something written on a page, the musician builds melody, harmony, and rhythm on the spot — sometimes called "composing in the moment."

A method of basing improvisation on a specific scale (mode) rather than a chord progression. With fewer harmonic changes within a piece, the player can explore the scale itself more freely — the core idea behind modal jazz.
Slang for holing up like it's a woodshed to practice intensively. The phrase captures the culture of disciplined effort behind building technique and phrase vocabulary.
A player who appears on another bandleader's recordings or tours rather than leading their own. Many great musicians built their careers as sidemen, moving between multiple groups.
A small group of roughly three to six players, as opposed to a big band. It became the standard performing format for improvisation-centered jazz after bebop.

An informal gathering where musicians play freely together without a fixed lineup or rehearsal. The 1940s jam sessions in Harlem (at venues like Minton's Playhouse) were the breeding ground for bebop.
Deliberately shifting rhythmic emphasis to accent weak beats. A fundamental technique behind jazz's sense of drive and swing.
The most common three-chord sequence in jazz harmony. Much of the theory behind improvised lines and substitute chords is built around this progression.
A short chord progression that leads smoothly from the end of a chorus back to its beginning. Used at the tune's midpoint, it drives momentum through cyclical chord forms.
How the notes of a given chord are arranged in pitch and order. One of the areas where a pianist's or arranger's individuality shows most clearly.
A technique that keeps an existing tune's melody intact while rewriting its chord progression. Often used to give a standard a fresh sound.
An improvisational approach that deliberately selects notes outside the current chord or key to build tension. Widely used by free jazz and post-bop players.
A specific phrase pattern or stock melodic fragment. Players build up a large vocabulary of licks and combine them in improvisation.
A technique of stating a short melodic fragment (a motif) and then transforming and repeating it to build an improvised solo. Sonny Rollins was known for his mastery of this approach.
The layering of different meters or rhythmic patterns at the same time. The complex rhythmic sensibility of African-derived music strongly shapes jazz drumming.
A saxophone or clarinet technique where the reed's vibration is stopped abruptly with the tongue to produce a popping sound. Widely used in swing-era section playing.

A technique on brass or reed instruments that produces a rasping, growling tone. Humming or vocalizing while playing creates a more human, expressive voice — the brass section of Duke Ellington's orchestra is the classic example.
A technique of fitting a device (a mute) into the bell of a brass instrument to alter its tone and volume. Different mutes, such as the Harmon mute on trumpet, yield a wide range of colors.
A technique of writing and singing lyrics that follow an instrumental melody or solo note-for-note. Groups like Lambert, Hendricks & Ross established the form.
The horn players in a band's lineup who stand in front of the rhythm section and carry the melody or solos. Trumpet, saxophone, and trombone typically fill this role.
An arrangement worked out through rehearsal and on-the-spot playing rather than written notation. Widely used by swing-era big bands such as Count Basie's orchestra.
A small combo with only a single horn player. This puts the spotlight on the leader's solos and highlights close dialogue with the rhythm section.
A combo lineup without a piano. Losing that harmonic anchor, the bass and horn players gain more freedom for contrapuntal interplay — the Gerry Mulligan Quartet is a classic example.
A technique of repeating a fixed melodic or rhythmic figure. In modal and free jazz, it provides a stable foundation beneath a shifting solo.
A short, repeated rhythmic melodic pattern. In swing-era big bands, a horn section repeating a riff behind the soloist became a standard technique.
A moment where the full ensemble stops playing for an instant and a single player fills the gap with a short unaccompanied phrase. It builds tension and is often used as an entry point into a solo.
A passage near the end of a piece where a soloist plays freely without accompaniment. Borrowed from classical music, it's a showcase for a soloist's technique.
A performance format where soloists alternate every four bars. Often used interchangeably with trading fours, though it's not limited to exchanges with the drummer and can involve multiple players.
A harmonic technique that replaces a given chord with another dominant seventh chord a tritone away. One of the basic tools of reharmonization since the bebop era.
A technique that borrows chords from a different mode of the same tonic. Used to bring unexpected color into a piece.
A rhythmic emphasis on the second and fourth beats of a four-beat bar. Marked on the hi-hat or snare drum, it's a fundamental element behind the feeling of swing.
A note played without clear attack — muted, faded, or barely sounded. A technique that adds rhythmic shading and groove to a phrase.
A scale that inserts one extra passing tone between chord tones to create an eight-note scale, so that beats and chord tones line up cleanly. Widely used by bebop-era players building fast lines.
A technique where the bass sustains or repeats a single note while the harmony above it continues to change. Used to build a climax or heighten tension.
A relaxed, unhurried feel created by placing notes slightly behind the beat. A subtle technique for generating groove without changing the actual tempo.
An original music theory proposed by Ornette Coleman. It treats harmony, melody, and rhythm as equal elements, aiming at playing unbound by fixed tonality.
A movement that sought to fuse classical composition technique with jazz improvisation. Proposed by Gunther Schuller and practiced by groups such as the Modern Jazz Quartet.
A term for jazz of the current era generally, made with a modern sensibility rather than tied to one fixed style. Often used more as a period marker than a genre label.
A way of building a phrase that starts from notes inside a chord, gradually ventures to notes outside it, and returns. It creates a narrative of tension and resolution within an improvised line.

A body of tunes written from the 1960s onward, distinct from the traditional Great American Songbook, that became established as jazz repertoire staples — pieces like "A Love Supreme" or "Maiden Voyage" fall into this category.
The written commentary included with a record or CD's packaging. It records background on the work and its performers, helping listeners understand what they're hearing.
